# 8 Types of Promotions to Drive Revenue During the Holidays \[2026\]


- by[Francesca Nicasio](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/author/francesca-nicasio/)
- 2026-11-16


minute read


Share Post

The holiday season is upon us, and for retailers and consumers alike, this means sales and discounts galore. For most retailers, promotions are a critical vehicle for attracting shoppers and generating demand.


And promotions clearly work. According to Lightspeed’s consumer survey,* **60.8% of respondents say better prices or sales would make them more likely to buy non-essential items** .


All that being said, the holiday season is the most competitive period for sales and promos, which is why you can’t just put out a “SALE” sign on your window and call it a day.


To maximize the results of your promos, you need to choose offers that fit your goals, products and customers. That’s exactly what we’ll discuss in this post. We’ll cover the types of promotions to run during the holiday season, how to choose the right discounts and best practices for implementing them.


- Types of holiday promotions to implement
- Holiday promotions that are not traditional discounts
- How to protect margins when running holiday discounts
- How to measure holiday discount performance
- Set up your promos for success this holiday season


#### Boost sales & win customers this holiday season


From stocking the right inventory to crafting marketing campaigns that sparkle, success starts with the right tools.


Get holiday ready with Lightspeed


## **Types of holiday promotions to implement**


Promos come in various forms. Here are some of the most common ones to consider.


### **1. Percentage-off discounts**


Percentage-off discounts reduce the price of an eligible item or group of products by a set percentage. They’re easy to understand and promote, but work best when tied to a specific goal.


**Where and how to apply them:** Apply them to selected seasonal items, slower-moving inventory, or a category you want to move. You can also reserve an offer for a specific customer group, such as loyalty members, instead of discounting the entire store.


A targeted markdown gives you more control than a storewide sale: you choose which products qualify and can exclude bestsellers or low-stock items that are already selling at full price. For example, offer 20% off selected seasonal apparel or gift categories while keeping high-demand products at regular price.


**Pro tip:** In Lightspeed Retail, you can[set an advanced promotion](https://x-series-support.lightspeedhq.com/hc/en-us/articles/25534113032859-Setting-up-multi-save-and-conditional-promotions) for selected products and outlets, then exclude items that shouldn’t be discounted. Use those controls to keep the offer focused on the stock you want to move.


Before setting the discount, calculate the resulting margin and establish a minimum you’re willing to accept. For example, an item priced at $100 with a $50 product cost would sell for $80 after a 20% discount, leaving a 37.5% gross margin before other costs. If that falls below your margin floor, reduce the discount or leave the item out of the promotion.


### **2. Dollar-off discounts**


Dollar-off discounts take a set amount off an item or an entire purchase. “Save $25” makes the savings clear at a glance.


**Where and how to apply them:** This format can work well on higher-priced products or as a spend-threshold offer that encourages shoppers to add another item to their basket.


To set a minimum spend, look at your typical transaction value and choose a threshold that encourages a larger purchase while keeping the offer achievable. Then check that the products customers are likely to add still leave enough margin after the discount. For example, “Save $25 when you spend $150” gives shoppers a clear incentive to reach the threshold. At $150, that discount is about 16.7% of the purchase.


Compare the offer with a percentage discount before choosing: on a $150 purchase, 20% off saves $30, so it’s a bigger discount than $25 off. On a $100 item, however, $25 off equals 25% off, while 20% off saves $20. Choose the format that makes the value easy to understand and fits your margin and basket-size goals.


### **3. Buy one get one (BOGO) and multi-buy promotions**


Buy-one, get-one (BOGO) promotions give shoppers a reward for purchasing a set number of items. Common variations include:


- Buy one, get one free.
- Buy one, get a second item 50% off.
- Buy two, get one free.
- Buy one, get a gift with purchase.


These offers can encourage shoppers to buy multiple units and help move selected inventory.


**Where and how to apply them:** They work best for products customers are likely to buy in multiples or give as small gifts, such as stocking stuffers, socks, accessories, beauty products, or wine. Retailers can also pair complementary items, as long as the offer makes sense for the products and their margins.


Use BOGO selectively rather than applying it across the store. Before launching, calculate the total discount at the quantities shoppers need to buy, set a minimum margin, and exclude high-demand or low-stock products.


For last-minute or post-holiday promotions, consider limiting the offer to seasonal merchandise you need to sell through. Make the terms clear, including which products qualify, whether the free or discounted item must be the lower-priced one, and any quantity limits.


### **4. Quantity and tiered discounts**


Quantity discounts reward shoppers with greater savings as they add more eligible items to their purchase. For example, “Buy 2, save 10%; buy 3 or more, save 15%” gives customers a reason to add another item without discounting every product in the store.


**Pro tip:** Lightspeed Retail[supports multi-save promotions](https://x-series-support.lightspeedhq.com/hc/en-us/articles/25534113032859-Setting-up-multi-save-and-conditional-promotions) . Be sure to check for overlap before launch. When promotions with different types or criteria apply to the same products, the first-created offer may take priority.


**Where and how to apply them:** This approach can work well for items shoppers often buy in multiples, such as greeting cards, ornaments, specialty foods, or small accessories. Set the tiers around products that support your goal, whether that’s growing basket size or moving selected inventory.


Before launching, check the margin at each tier, especially the highest discount, and limit eligibility if needed. Keep the rules simple: use only a few tiers, make clear which products count, and state whether the discount applies to all qualifying items or only additional units. Avoid complicated exclusions or stacking rules that are hard to explain at checkout.


### **5. Bundles and gifts with purchase**


Bundles bring complementary products together at one price, making it easier for shoppers to find a ready-made gift. Organize them by recipient, interest, use, or budget, such as a beginner’s craft kit, a host gift set, or a bundle under $50.


**Where and how to apply them:** Pair a bestseller with a product that complements it, including a slower-moving item when it makes sense for the shopper. The combination should feel useful, not like a way to offload unrelated stock.


A gift-with-purchase offer adds a free item when a shopper buys a qualifying product or reaches a spending threshold. Retailers might include a small accessory with a purchase or offer a seasonal gift when customers spend a certain amount. Ready-to-gift packaging or an exclusive seasonal set can add appeal without reducing the price of every item.


To protect margin, calculate the cost and margin of the complete bundle or free gift before setting the offer. Make the value clear: list what’s included, show the bundle price alongside individual prices when applicable, and state any qualifying purchase or availability limits. This helps shoppers understand the offer before they reach checkout.


### **6. Spend-threshold and free-shipping offers**


Spend-threshold promotions reward customers when their purchase reaches a set amount. Examples include “Spend $100, save $15,” free shipping on orders over $75, or a free gift or bonus loyalty points when shoppers spend a certain amount. Because customers may add another item to qualify, these offers can encourage larger baskets.


**Where and how to apply them:** Set the threshold using your own order data. If your typical order is $80, setting a $100 minimum may encourage shoppers to add another $20 worth of products. Make sure that threshold feels attainable and that the added items still support your margin. For a “Spend $100, save $15” offer, the discount is 15% at the minimum spend; on a $120 order, it’s 12.5%. Check the effective discount at likely basket sizes and confirm the offer still leaves enough margin.


Free shipping can be compelling, but the order minimum should account for shipping, packaging, and fulfillment costs. If free shipping isn’t viable, consider alternatives such as in-store pickup or local delivery where your operations support them. State the minimum spend, eligible products, and delivery or pickup terms clearly wherever shoppers see the offer.


### **7. Loyalty and exclusive customer offers**


Use loyalty rewards to recognize existing customers and give holiday shoppers a reason to return. Lightspeed’s research shows that 40.3% of shoppers say in-store-only loyalty rewards bring them back.


With that in mind, retailers might offer bonus points on seasonal purchases, run a double-points day, or give members early access to a sale or an exclusive discount. A coupon or reward for a future purchase can extend the relationship beyond the holiday transaction. For example, a shopper who earns bonus points in December could redeem them on a January visit.


**Where and how to apply them:** Tailor the offer to the customer. Loyal members may value early access or an extra reward; new customers might respond to a welcome incentive for their next purchase; and lapsed customers may need a targeted offer to give them a reason to come back. Avoid sending the same discount to everyone when a different perk could be more relevant. Make redemption rules and expiration dates clear, and track whether the offer leads to repeat visits or purchases after the holidays.


### **8. Flash sales and time-limited discounts**


A flash sale offers a discount for a short, clearly defined period. A real deadline gives shoppers a reason to act now, while a limited product selection can help retailers focus attention on specific inventory.


**Where and how to use them:** Use flash sales for a particular purpose, such as bringing shoppers in during a quieter day, moving excess seasonal stock, or highlighting last-minute gifts. Examples include a 24-hour online promotion, a rotating “12 days of deals” campaign, a one-day last-minute gift offer, or a post-holiday clearance event.


Promote the sale ahead of time so customers know when it starts, what’s included, and when it ends. Before launching, confirm that inventory, staffing, and fulfillment can support the expected demand. Keep the promotion occasional and tied to a clear goal rather than discounting constantly; frequent sales can make shoppers less inclined to buy at full price. Honor the stated deadline and make exclusions or quantity limits easy to find.


## **Holiday promotions that are not traditional discounts**


A promotion doesn’t have to lower the product price to give shoppers a reason to buy. Value-add offers can make shopping easier, add a thoughtful extra, or give customers more flexibility without applying a blanket markdown. Depending on your operations, consider:


- **Gift cards:** They bring in revenue when purchased and give recipients a reason to visit your store after the holidays.
- **Flexible payment options:** Buy now, pay later or other payment plans can help shoppers manage larger purchases. Review provider fees and terms before promoting them.
- **Free gift wrapping:** Add convenience for gift buyers, while accounting for materials and staff time.
- **Extended returns:** Give holiday shoppers more time to make returns, and clearly explain the eligible products and return window.
- **Buy online, pick up in store:** Offer a convenient fulfillment choice when inventory visibility and store capacity can support it.
- **Early access:** Give loyalty members or another defined customer group first access to new products, limited-edition items, or a seasonal sale.


These incentives have costs and operational requirements of their own, so choose those that fit your customers and business. State the terms clearly, including eligibility, timing, fees, and fulfillment or return details where relevant.


## **How to protect margins when running holiday discounts**


Discounts can lift sales, but they also reduce what you earn on each eligible item. Set a clear goal, then use sales, inventory, and margin data to choose the products in the promotion.


Before launching:


- **Choose products strategically.** Use targeted markdowns to support your goal, such as moving slow-selling seasonal stock. Don’t automatically discount products already selling well at full price.


**Pro tip:** Use[Lightspeed’s inventory reports](https://x-series-support.lightspeedhq.com/hc/en-us/articles/25534093525915-Basic-and-advanced-reporting-in-Retail-POS-X-Series) to spot slow-moving items before choosing products for a targeted offer. Depending on your plan, reports such as sell-through and dusty inventory can help inform markdown decisions.


- **Set a margin floor.** Calculate the margin at the discounted price, and account for any offers that can be combined.
- **Make the terms clear.** Define eligible products, exclusions, quantity limits, and the promotion’s start and end dates.


While the promotion is running:


- Track units sold, sell-through, redemptions, and gross margin against a relevant baseline.
- If the offer isn’t moving the intended inventory, revisit the eligible products or promotion before deepening the discount.
- Consider a bundle, loyalty reward, or gift with purchase as an alternative.


Broad, aggressive markdowns can reduce profit and may encourage shoppers to wait for sales. Keep each discount targeted and tied to a business goal.


## **How to measure holiday discount performance**


Don’t judge a promotion by revenue alone. Track a mix of sales, margin, inventory, and customer metrics to see whether the offer met its goal.


**Sales and basket size**


- Revenue and units sold.
- Average order value and items per transaction.
- Promotion redemption rate.


**Profit and inventory**


- Gross margin after the discount and total discount cost.
- Sell-through of eligible products.
- Inventory remaining after the promotion.


**Customer and campaign results**


- New customers acquired and repeat purchases after the promotion.
- Loyalty sign-ups and reward redemptions.
- Campaign clicks and attributed sales, where tracking is available.


Compare results with a relevant baseline, such as a similar period or comparable products that weren’t promoted. Consider both immediate sales and margin impact, as well as whether the promotion brings customers back after the holidays.


**Pro tip:** Depending on your plan,[Lightspeed Retail reports](https://x-series-support.lightspeedhq.com/hc/en-us/articles/25534093525915-Basic-and-advanced-reporting-in-Retail-POS-X-Series) can show sales by promotion alongside revenue, gross profit, margin, and discount measures. Advanced reporting adds inventory views such as sell-through, so you can assess both the offer and its effect on stock.


## **Set up your promos for success this holiday season**


The holiday period is high time for sales and promos. Maximize your results by selecting the right offers and implementing them at the right time.
